study.title: 1 Chronicles 3 The lineage of David, the monarchy of Judah, and the preserved hope
study.overview: The chapter records David's offspring in three movements: his sons born in Hebron, the children born in Jerusalem, and the royal line that goes from Solomon until the later period of exile. The list is not only genealogical; it shows how the promise made to David's house goes through family failures, political succession, national judgment and historical survival. The text highlights both the honor of lineage and its vulnerability, culminating in the preservation of names linked to the people of God even after the fall of the kingdom.

outline.title: The sons of David in Hebron
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with six sons born to David as he reigned in Hebron. The list shows the fecundity of the royal house and also the tense domestic setting surrounding this family, as some of these children appear in other parts of the Bible as figures of conflict. Observation of the years of reign in Hebron and Jerusalem places genealogy in the concrete history of David's reign.

outline.title: The children in Jerusalem and the succession of the kings of Judah
outline.explanation: In Jerusalem, David has other children, including Solomon. From Solomon, the genealogy proceeds to accompany the line of the kings of Judah to exile, showing a continual succession between promise and responsibility. The record includes kings known for fidelity and infidelity, remembering that dynastic continuity does not prevent divine judgment.

outline.title: The descent after exile to the generation of the chronicler
outline.explanation: After the deportation, the list continues with the descendants of Jeconiah and then with Zorobabel, reaching names that show the stay of David's family after the national catastrophe. The chapter ends with a chain of descent that reaches the time of the chronicler, indicating that the lineage was not interrupted despite exile. The conclusion holds the memory of the divine promise beyond political ruin.

study.context: The notes provided say that this passage continues the genealogy of Ram and that he divides David's family into three sections: sons of David, kings of Judah to exile and descendants of Jeconiah until the time of the chronicler. They also report that the focus falls on Solomon's line and Nathan's line, and that the list aims to preserve the memory of David's house after deportation. There are no safe additional data on the exact date of composition, detailed geography or historical circumstances beyond the genealogy chain itself.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God leads history through real family lines, without ceasing to treat sin seriously. The house of David is presented as honored, but not idealized: there are troublesome children, faithful kings and unfaithful kings, and an exile that interrupts the visible monarchy. Still, the genealogy does not end in the collapse, but goes on, which suggests providential preservation of the promise. From the evangelical Christian point of view, it is legitimate to see here the historical frame that prepares the coming of the Messiah, as the notes observe that Christ came from this family according to the flesh. At the same time, the text values God's faithfulness more than human merit, because the continuity of lineage depends on divine action and not only on the capacity of kings.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter is divided into three parts: the sons of David, the kings of Judah to exile, and the descendants of Jeconiah until about four hundred years before Christ. This shows that genealogy serves to link David's house to the later history of Israel.

David's lineage is presented as the most illustrious of Israel, and the note highlights that Christ came according to the flesh. The genealogy of the kings goes from Solomon to exile, showing the continuity of the promise despite human failures.

Observation on the last name indicates that some readings link Anani to a Messianic expectation, although this appears as a traditional interpretation and not as a certainty of the text. The commentator also notes variations in manuscripts in this part of the genealogy.

questions: What does the preservation of David's lineage teach about God's faithfulness even when leaders fail?
Why does the chronicler include both well-known kings and lesser known names after exile?
How does this genealogy prepare the reader to understand the Messianic hope in the rest of the Scriptures?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a memory of God's faithfulness through imperfect generations. As you reflect on your own family and your church, consider that the value before God does not depend on human prestige, but on staying in the covenant and obedience. This passage also invites to honor the history of faith: forgotten names in the eyes of the world can continue to be important before God. Apply this by cultivating gratitude for the spiritual inheritance received and a commitment not to interrupt, for neglect or sin, what God wants to continue through you.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided limit historical reading to few general statements; therefore, it is not safe to detail dates, locations or identify with certainty all genealogical parallels outside the chapter itself. There are also divergent interpretative observations about some names, especially at the end of the list, and the text does not allow to transform these readings into indisputable facts.
